Compare word use against an explicit reference corpus

Source: vignettes/keyness-comparison.Rmd
keyness-comparison.Rmd

Which words occur relatively more often in one corpus than in another? The answer depends on the reference: its genres, topics, writers and collection conditions help determine what a difference means. Keyness describes that comparison; it does not by itself measure language proficiency or writing quality.

This guide uses ldfreq 0.3.0.9011 or later. The explicitly sourced helpers in examples/keyness.R retain both corpora, the tokens counted, the two-by-two tables, and links back to the original text. They are installed examples, not exported functions. Counting needs no optional package; returning to KWIC uses quanteda >= 4.5.0. The inputs below are authored for checking calculations, not learner data or an evaluation of annotation accuracy.

Declare the documents and inspect the coverage 

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "keyness-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
comparison <- demo$comparison
knitr::kable(comparison$totals[c("corpus", "documents", "source_tokens",
  "missing_terms", "counted_tokens")], row.names = FALSE)
corpus documents source_tokens missing_terms counted_tokens
target 3 10 1 8
reference 3 8 0 8

The target is t1, t2, t_empty; the reference is r1, r2, r_empty. Both have 8 counted tokens. The target has 10 original tokens: a period is excluded and one retained token has no lemma. The document outside is not in either corpus. Empty documents remain declared documents; they do not supply tokens to the denominator.

knitr::kable(demo$annotations$segments[c("document_id", "text")], row.names = FALSE)
document_id text
t1 learn learn learn learn read .
t2 learn learn write unknown
t_empty
r1 learn read read read
r2 learn read read speak
r_empty
outside unlisted unlisted

For your own unchanged lexdiv_import_annotations() result, source both helpers explicitly. The concordance guide explains how to prepare complete, aligned annotations with original offsets.

helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
for (file in c("concordance.R", "keyness.R"))
  sys.source(system.file("examples", file, package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
comparison <- helper$keyness_compare(annotations,
  target = target_document_ids, reference = reference_document_ids,
  preprocessing_id = "lemma-exclude-punctuation-v1",
  term_col = "lemma", keep = keep)

target and reference must each contain unique, known document IDs, with no ID shared between them. Unlisted documents are explicitly excluded rather than silently becoming the reference. keep has one non-missing logical value per original token, including tokens in excluded documents. Define the same unit and selection policy for both corpora, and name that policy in preprocessing_id. This label does not execute preprocessing: the saved annotation metadata and mask record what was actually supplied.

Terms use exact UTF-8 values of term_col, with no added case folding, Unicode normalization or lemmatization. Missing and whitespace-only terms cannot be counted. The vocabulary is the union of counted terms in the two corpora; a term absent from both has no row. Differences between annotation tools or selection policies can create apparent keyness. Inspect those conditions before interpreting a corpus contrast.

$token_audit records each token’s corpus, selection, availability and counting status. $documents retains source, retained, missing and counted token totals for every document. It also flags documents whose ordered original segment texts are identical across groups. This includes matching empty documents. The flag does not detect near duplicates or identical text split into different segments, and does not remove anything. Resolve substantive overlap in your corpus design and repeat the comparison if its membership changes.

Read counts before scores 

counts <- comparison$results
knitr::kable(counts[c("term", "target_count", "reference_count",
  "target_documents", "reference_documents")], row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Term", "Target tokens", "Reference tokens", "Target documents", "Reference documents"))
Term Target tokens Reference tokens Target documents Reference documents
learn 6 2 2 2
read 1 5 1 2
write 1 0 1 0
speak 0 1 0 1

learn occurs 6 times in the target and twice in the reference. Its table includes all other counted terms, not just words chosen for display:

word <- subset(counts, term == "learn")
table2 <- rbind(target = c(word$target_count, word$target_other),
  reference = c(word$reference_count, word$reference_other))
colnames(table2) <- c("learn", "All other terms")
knitr::kable(table2)
learn All other terms
target 6 2
reference 2 6

For each cell, expected count E is its row total times its column total, divided by the grand total. Here all four expectations are 4. The uncorrected likelihood-ratio statistic is G² = 2 sum[O log(O / E)], using natural logarithms and a contribution of zero when O = 0. This is the comparison of a shared word probability with separate corpus probabilities described by Dunning (1993, Section 5.3). Every observed and expected cell is retained in $results.

knitr::kable(counts[c("term", "target_per_1000", "reference_per_1000", "log_ratio")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Term", "Target per 1,000", "Reference per 1,000", "Log2 ratio"))
Term Target per 1,000 Reference per 1,000 Log2 ratio
learn 750 250 1.5850
read 125 625 -2.3219
write 125 0 Inf
speak 0 125 -Inf 
knitr::kable(counts[c("term", "G2", "signed_G2", "direction")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
term G2 signed_G2 direction
learn 4.1860 4.1860 target
read 4.5567 -4.5567 reference
write 1.4530 1.4530 target
speak 1.4530 -1.4530 reference
  • G2 is nonnegative. signed_G2 adds the direction of the rate difference: positive for the target, negative for the reference, zero for equal rates. The negative value is a ranking convention, not a negative chi-squared statistic.
  • log_ratio is log2(target_count / target_total) - log2(reference_count / reference_total). A value of 1 means twice the rate; -1 means half. For learn, the rates are 750 and 250 per 1,000, giving log2(3), approximately 1.585.
  • G² changes with the amount of data even when rates stay the same. Read it beside raw counts, rates, log-ratio and document frequencies, not as an effect-size measure alone.

No continuity correction or smoothing is applied. An observed zero in just one corpus produces a finite G² and an infinite log-ratio (Inf or -Inf). That infinity describes a sample zero, not evidence for an unlimited population effect. If either corpus has no counted tokens, the comparison scores are NA with empty_target or empty_reference status. With both empty, $results has no rows and $totals$status explains why. If a term accounts for every counted token in both nonempty corpora, its rates are equal and its scores are zero (constant_feature). Missing annotations never become known zero counts.

These helpers produce descriptive scores, without p-values or significance decisions. Tokens within documents, repeated texts from one writer, and words examined in the same search are not independent study observations. Ranking many words also selects extreme contrasts. Do not interpret this table as adjusted multiple testing or as a substitute for a model that addresses the research design. Preserve writer, task and occasion IDs using the repeated-observations workflow.

Select rows while retaining the original comparison 

selected <- helper$keyness_compare(comparison$source,
  target = comparison$settings$target, reference = comparison$settings$reference,
  preprocessing_id = comparison$settings$preprocessing_id,
  term_col = comparison$settings$term_col, keep = comparison$settings$keep,
  min_count = 2L)
shown <- subset(selected$results, meets_min_count)
shown <- shown[order(-shown$signed_G2), ]
knitr::kable(shown[c("term", "target_count", "reference_count", "signed_G2")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
term target_count reference_count signed_G2
learn 6 2 4.1860
read 1 5 -4.5567

min_count is a positive whole number applied to pooled frequency. It only changes a display flag: the vocabulary, counts, background terms and denominators remain complete. Its default of 1 allows singletons to be inspected; it is not a recommendation to rank rare terms without scrutiny. Changing keep, in contrast, changes which tokens contribute to both the counts and denominators.

$document_counts stores positive counts by document, corpus and term without allocating a dense document-by-vocabulary table. To inspect a selected word, join these counts to $documents, retaining declared empty documents. A missing row there means no counted occurrence; consult the token coverage before treating that as complete observation of the word’s absence.

Return to exactly the counted occurrences 

context <- helper$keyness_concordance(comparison, "learn", window = 2L)
hits <- context$search$occurrences
hits$corpus <- comparison$documents$corpus[
  match(hits$document_id, comparison$documents$document_id)]
knitr::kable(hits[c("document_id", "corpus", "pre", "keyword", "post")], row.names = FALSE)
document_id corpus pre keyword post
t1 target learn learn learn
t1 target learn learn learn learn
t1 target learn learn learn learn read
t1 target learn learn learn read .
t2 target learn learn write
t2 target learn learn write unknown
r1 reference learn read read
r2 reference learn read read 
stopifnot(sum(hits$corpus == "target") == word$target_count,
  sum(hits$corpus == "reference") == word$reference_count)

This search uses the saved counting mask and one exact term, including its case and Unicode form. It returns 6 target and 2 reference occurrences of learn. The KWIC shows original surface text even when counting lemmas; excluded or missing nearby tokens still appear in the context. Original document/segment IDs, token indices and inclusive character offsets connect each match to the source. The returned comparison_id identifies its comparison. Use a UTF-8 LC_CTYPE locale for non-ASCII KWIC terms, as required by the adapter.

By default, max_tokens = 1e6 bounds the complete source passed to keyness_compare(), before exclusions. KWIC’s separate max_cells = 1e6 bounds stored matches and context cells as in the concordance guide. Exceeding either bound raises an error instead of truncating the analysis. These limits are not a guarantee of total memory use or a streaming large-corpus implementation.

Save the reasons, source and complete result 

record <- list(comparison = comparison,
  target_reason = "Authored target documents for checking the calculation",
  reference_reason = "Disjoint authored reference with known counts",
  session = sessionInfo())
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") # use a durable project path for your analysis
saveRDS(record, file, version = 2)
reopened <- readRDS(file)
helper$keyness_validate(reopened$comparison)
s <- reopened$comparison$settings
replayed <- helper$keyness_compare(reopened$comparison$source,
  target = s$target, reference = s$reference, preprocessing_id = s$preprocessing_id,
  term_col = s$term_col, keep = s$keep, min_count = s$min_count, max_tokens = s$max_tokens)
stopifnot(identical(replayed, reopened$comparison))
unlink(file)

Record why the target and reference answer your question, including their collection and overlap checks. A different reference is a different comparison: repeat the calculation, keep both records, and explain the change. A selected CSV alone cannot reconstruct the background denominator. Validation detects accidental edits, not the authenticity or quality of supplied annotations. Exact whole-object replay requires the same package/helper version; after an upgrade, compare counts and settings explicitly.

Numerical checks and their scope

Hand counts and separate binomial log-likelihood calculations check the formula. Across 544 small two-by-two tables, including zero cells, unequal corpus sizes and equal rates, signed G² agrees within 1e-7 with quanteda.textstats 0.97.2 using measure = "lr", correction = "none". Specify that correction explicitly when comparing implementations. Its logarithms use a small numerical offset, so exact ties can differ slightly from zero. The independent likelihood calculation agrees within 1e-12. quanteda.textstats is not required to run this example, and its p-values are not imported.

These are counting and numerical checks on constructed inputs, not evidence that a reference corpus represents a population or that a word contrast measures proficiency. This example compares single annotated terms. For nearby-word association, use the separate collocation guide, whose population consists of token pairs rather than corpus word totals.
